summary:
Asteroid watch is an interactive planetary defense game designed for children ages 9–12. Inspired by NASA’s DART (Double Asteroid Redirection Test) mission, the game challenges players to protect Earth by learning how to detect, investigate, and redirect potentially dangerous asteroids.
Players take on the role of young planetary defense engineers and progress through three core stages: observing asteroids and analyzing their characteristics, designing a spacecraft by balancing components such as mass, propulsion, and navigation systems, and simulating a kinetic impact to see how it changes an asteroid’s trajectory. Through hands-on experiments, limited-resource decisions, and iterative testing, players learn that successful engineering requires evidence-based reasoning and adapting solutions to different challenges.
This project introduces concepts in astronomy, physics, and engineering accessible and engaging to children. More importantly, it encourages scientific curiosity, critical thinking, problem-solving, and an understanding of how space technology can help protect our planet.
details:
Asteroid Watch is an interactive browser game for elementary school students, designed to make planetary defense and spacecraft engineering easier to explore. Inspired by NASA’s Double Asteroid Redirection Test (DART), the game places players in a fictional mission: an asteroid may approach Earth in about eight years, and the team must decide what to learn, how to design a spacecraft, and whether its mission succeeds.

Players begin by investigating the asteroid. They choose observations using methods and facilities inspired by real astronomy, including NASA’s Infrared Telescope Facility and Goldstone radar. Each investigation reveals clues about the asteroid, such as its size, spin, material, shape, or path. Some jobs can happen at the same time, while jobs that need the same observing resource compete for its availability. Players manage the mission clock as they decide which evidence to gather.

Next, players bring their asteroid fact file to the Research Lab, where they spend mission time learning about DART-related technologies. In the design workbench, they choose cameras, solar arrays, propulsion, and communications equipment. A live five-axis radar chart shows how each choice changes spacecraft performance, and a game-generated success percentage updates with the configuration. Players then assemble their selected components and launch the spacecraft. A simulated mission-control view shows the spacecraft’s encounter and the asteroid’s resulting path.

The game encourages students to weigh evidence, manage limited time, and think about how engineering choices affect an entire system. Its interactive format gives them room to experiment and learn from outcomes. The success percentage introduces probability as a useful estimate rather than a guarantee.

We built the prototype with HTML, CSS, and JavaScript and published it on GitHub Pages so it can be played in a web browser. NASA and JPL resources, along with published research, informed the mission story, observation methods, and spacecraft components. The asteroid scenario, time costs, radar scores, and success probabilities are simplified values created for the game; they are not NASA predictions or real mission assessments.

The real DART mission targeted Dimorphos, a moonlet of the asteroid Didymos. Neither object threatened Earth. Asteroid Watch adapts DART’s kinetic-impact concept to a fictional Earth-threat scenario for educational purposes.
